description: STEAM team, with different knowledge and skills, great attitude and happy people.
summary: Asclepius is a daily health companion for astronauts on long missions. Each astronaut completes a short check-in and simple self-tests (reaction time, visual acuity and an Amsler grid). Asclepius combines them with simulated wearable, blood, urine and habitat data, and compares everything with the astronaut’s own normal values instead of generic thresholds. It tells the astronaut in plain words whether everything looks fine, what to watch and when to report to the crew medical officer, and it points out behavior patterns such as fewer conversations than usual or several long workdays with rising stress. Mental health data stays under the astronaut’s control: the medical officer sees only a status unless the astronaut chooses to share more. A mission environment selector (orbit station, deep-space transit, lunar base, Mars base) adapts radiation, dust risks and communication delay. Our team built it to learn across disciplines, combining software development with health-science input from a teammate who studies pharmacy.
details:
What it does. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting health changes in themselves. Asclepius helps them do that every day and decide when to involve the crew medical officer.

  • Today: one status line (no issues detected / watch / report to the medical officer recommended) with the reasons in plain words, the tasks due today and suggested actions.
  • Check-in: a 30-second form for mood, stress, energy, connection with crew and family, work hours and symptoms.
  • Tests: reaction time (a simplified Psychomotor Vigilance Test), visual acuity and an Amsler grid, to track fatigue and vision changes over time. They support tracking, not diagnosis.
  • Trends and patterns: charts against the astronaut’s own normal range, plus deterministic pattern rules such as isolation, sleep and mood, workload and declining mood.
  • Report to the medical officer: the astronaut chooses what to share. A private journal is never shared.
  • Medical officer view: crew overview, prioritized alerts, reports and follow-ups, with mental health shown only as a status unless the astronaut shares more.
  • Mission environments: orbit station, deep-space transit, lunar base and Mars base change the radiation background, add dust-related symptoms on surfaces, and adapt advice to the communication delay with Earth.

How it works. The app is rule-based and explainable; no machine learning makes decisions.

  1. A personal baseline (mean and standard deviation) is learned for each measure during the first mission week.
  2. Trend rules flag 3-day averages 2 or 3 standard deviations from the person’s normal; threshold rules apply fixed limits (NASA radiation and CO₂ limits; blood pressure, blood and urine ranges suggested by a teammate who studies pharmacy).
  3. A combined early-illness rule watches small simultaneous changes in resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, skin temperature, leukocytes, lymphocytes and sleep; in the demo it warns two days before a simulated fever.
  4. Alerts have four levels (no issues, watch, alert, urgent); urgent rules cover a solar particle event, low blood oxygen and fever with shortness of breath.
  5. A privacy function decides what each role can see; every access by the medical officer is logged and visible to the astronaut.
  6. Automated tests check the privacy rules and the demo scenarios, and an “Alert performance” page reports detection on the simulated mission.

Benefits and goals. Earlier awareness of health changes, guidance written for non-specialists, more autonomy when Earth is minutes away, and protection of mental health privacy in a small crew. The same approach could help isolated teams on Earth, such as Antarctic stations or remote communities with limited access to doctors.

Limitations. All crew data is simulated and fictional. Thresholds are provisional and need clinical validation. Asclepius is a prototype for learning and is not a medical device.

Why we built it. We joined Space Apps to learn from each other across disciplines, not to build the most optimized product. Teammates from software learned about space medicine, and our pharmacy student learned how health criteria become software.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, Recharts, Vitest, Git and GitHub, GitHub Pages for hosting, Visual Studio Code, GitHub Copilot and Claude (see “Use of Super Intelligence (SI)”).
